record.paper_title: K3: A New Problem List in Low-Dimensional Topology
record.original_question: For a knot K in the 3-sphere, let u(K) be its unknotting number, the minimum number of crossing changes needed over all diagrams of K to obtain the unknot. Does the connected sum of n nontrivial knots always have unknotting number at least n? Is unknotting number invariant under Conway mutation, the operation of removing a 4-ended tangle from a link and replacing it after a 180-degree rotation that interchanges the endpoints in pairs?

evidence.quote: The unknotting number u(K) of a knot K in S^3 is the minimum, taken over all diagrams of K, of the number of crossings that must be changed to obtain a diagram of the unknot.
Conway mutation is the operation of removing a portion of a link that hits a 2-sphere in 4 points, and replacing it after a 180 degree rotation around an axis (interchanging the points in pairs).

Problem 1.3. How does unknotting number behave under connected sum and mutation? (a) Does the connected sum of n nontrivial knots have unknotting number at least n? (b) Is unknotting number invariant under mutation?

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Let K be a knot in the 3-sphere S^3. The unknotting number u(K) is defined as the minimum, taken over all planar diagrams D of K, of the number of crossing changes that must be performed in D in order to transform it into a diagram of the unknot. A Conway mutation of a link L is the operation of choosing an embedded 2-sphere S in S^3 that meets L transversely in exactly 4 points, removing the tangle (B, B∩L) on one side (where B is the 3-ball bounded by S), and re-gluing it after a 180-degree rotation about one of the three coordinate axes that permutes the four boundary points in pairs.

Answer the following two questions:

(a) For every integer n ≥ 1 and every collection K_1, …, K_n of nontrivial knots in S^3, does the connected sum satisfy
   u(K_1 # K_2 # ⋯ # K_n) ≥ n?

(b) Is the unknotting number invariant under Conway mutation? That is, if a knot K' is obtained from a knot K by a single Conway mutation, must u(K') = u(K)?
artifact.status_search_result: Both parts appear to remain open as of 2026. In 2025, Brittenham and Hermiller showed that unknotting number is not additive under connected sum (e.g., u(7_1 # mirror(7_1)) ≤ 5 while each summand has unknotting number 3), resolving the long-standing additivity conjecture in the negative. However, this counterexample does not contradict the weaker bound u(K_1 # ⋯ # K_n) ≥ n, and the question of whether the unknotting number of a connected sum of n nontrivial knots is at least n remains open, as does the question of whether unknotting number is invariant under Conway mutation.

status_evidence.title: Unknotting number is not additive under connected sum
status_evidence.snippet: First examples are given where u(K_1 # K_2) < u(K_1) + u(K_2), disproving additivity but not the weaker lower-bound conjecture.
status_evidence.claim: Additivity of unknotting number under connected sum fails; the strict bound u(#K_i) ≥ n remains unresolved by this counterexample.

status_evidence.title: A Simple Way To Measure Knots Has Come Unraveled — Quanta Magazine
status_evidence.snippet: The additivity conjecture for unknotting number, dating to 1937, was disproved in 2025.
status_evidence.claim: Additivity was only just disproved in 2025, so the more refined questions about ≥ n behavior and mutation invariance are still discussed as open.

status_evidence.title: The unknotting number, hard unknot diagrams, and reinforcement learning (Lackenby)
status_evidence.snippet: Discusses open problems on unknotting number, including its behavior under connected sum and mutation.
status_evidence.claim: Mutation invariance of unknotting number is listed as an open problem.
